scenes.heading: Circles: circumference and area
scenes.say: How far does a bike travel when its wheel turns once? Is one big pizza more than two small ones? To answer these, you need a special number called pi.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Roll a can one full turn: it goes just over 3 times its width
scenes.science: For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter = π ≈ 3.14
scenes.breaks: Measuring a can only gives π roughly; its true decimals go on forever without repeating.
scenes.say: Mark the rim of a can and roll it one full turn. It travels a bit more than three times its width. That a bit more than three is the same for every circle. It is called pi, about three point one four.
scenes.caption: Roll a can one full turn and it travels a bit more than 3 times its width. That number is the same for every circle: π ≈ 3.14.

scenes.heading: Parts of a circle
scenes.say: First the circle and its centre, O. Then the diameter, straight across through the centre, and the radius, from the centre to the edge. The diameter is two radii. The distance around the outside is the circumference.

scenes.heading: Circumference
scenes.say: The circumference is pi times the diameter, or two times pi times the radius. They are the same thing, because the diameter is two radii.
scenes.caption: C = πd, or C = 2πr. They are the same thing, because d = 2r.

scenes.heading: Why the area is πr²
notes: Cut the circle into thin slices
Height r, base half the circumference πr
scenes.say: Cut a circle into thin slices and lay them top to tail. They make a shape that is almost a parallelogram. Its height is the radius, and its base is half the circumference, pi r. So the area is pi r times r, which is pi r squared.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Find the area of a circle with radius 6 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
scenes.say: A circle has radius six centimetres. Square the radius first: thirty-six. So the exact area is thirty-six pi. Using three point one four, that is about one hundred and thirteen point zero four square centimetres.
scenes.caption: Radius 6 cm. Square the radius first: 36. Exact area = 36π. Using 3.14, that is about 113.04 cm².

scenes.heading: Circumference or area?
scenes.say: Don't mix them up. Circumference is the distance around, pi d, measured in centimetres. Area is the space inside, pi r squared, in square centimetres. For semicircles and quarter circles, remember to add the straight edges to the perimeter.

Quick recap. The diameter is two radii, and pi is about three point one four. Circumference is pi d. Area is pi r squared, squaring only the radius. Exact answers keep pi. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Quick recap. d = 2r, π ≈ 3.14. C = πd. A = πr², squaring only r. Exact answers keep π. Now try the practice questions!
